utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would recall Ambassador Pasic -- or, Your Honour, the Prosecution had also requested that a decision on the 29 bis be expedited and I am prepared to make oral argument of that or any time today the Chamber would wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's get on with the witness first and we'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago before a minute or so I received this binder for the witness after this one, and he's also under 92 bis, which in fact means that there won't be a live witness passing through these documents but that it would be up to me to assume and guess what's inside them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry you've been kept waiting all yesterday. Mr. Milosevic, as far as that's concerned, we'll deal with it -- let's deal with this witness first and then we'll come back and look at that witness and the binder, which we don't have yet, but we'll look at it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just note for the record it's just a re-disclosure of materials that were originally provided on the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us return to it after we finish this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ambassador Pasic, we interrupted your testimony the other day when you were describing a visit to President Cosic's office. Before I ask you to continue on that topic, I would like to return to clarify a point that you made about interviews that you had with members of the Serbian MUP. And the point I would like to clarify is, did any of these interviews -- were you ever required to actually go to the offices of the Serbian MUP to have these interviews?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And with what frequency during this time period were you required to go to the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very frequently, as I said last time, mostly on Mondays.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would happen on a typical Monday interview that you would have at the -- in the building of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what it looked like: I would go up to the reception desk, somebody would come to fetch me, take me to one of the offices, and they asked me there about all the contacts I had with people who they thought were important people, and they knew everything about me, and very often there was repetition. They'd ask me what they'd asked me the previous time. They asked me about my friends and everything else. And before Mr. Milosevic came to power, they would come to me from Bosnia or from abroad or from wherever. So those were the questions that I was asked mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can return to your visit to President Cosic's office, if I understood you correctly, you described being in a waiting room with several other people, the waiting room being outside the direct office of President Cosic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The waiting room was in front of the office, there was another door that was open in front, as I said. There were quite a lot of people wearing uniforms, military ones and not only military uniforms but from Bosnia, Croatia, et cetera. There were also officers of the Yugoslav People's Army there too and they were engaged in a heated discussion. They held some documents in their hands, some maps and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the Federal Minister of Foreign Affairs present in the waiting room during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would be Mr. Jovanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How far away was Mr. Jovanovic from where you were sitting in the waiting room?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, one to two metres, three perhaps, and so on, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Mr. Jovanovic had a phone conversation with somebody in the waiting room?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while we were waiting in the waiting room, Mr. Jovanovic -- actually, you could say he was on the telephone all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And based upon what you could hear Mr. Jovanovic saying, did you reach some conclusion about who it was he was speaking with?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From what I was able to hear, Mr. Jovanovic would frequently use the following sentences: "Yes, Mr. President." "Yes, President Slobo." "Yes, I'll convey that to Karadzic." "Yes, President, yes." And this -- and this sentence to the letter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you to slow down a little bit, Ambassador Pasic. So I could ask you to do that and could you please repeat the last part of your last answer. They missed some of it. So if you could repeat some of the dialogue you recall Jovanovic saying.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. Jovanovic was on the telephone, and as far as I was able to hear at the time, this is what he said, quite literally: "Yes, yes, Mr. President. Yes, President Slobo. I'll convey that to Karadzic, yes. Yes. I won't allow that stupid Buha to get in front of the microphone. Yes." That's what I was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long did that telephone conversation last?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several telephone conversations. They were interrupted and then they continued. I only heard these segments from those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how long was the conversation on the telephone that you believed was referring to President Slobodan, or that you're saying the word "President Slobo." How long was that conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of conversations, and my impression was that all the conversations were conducted with Mr. Milosevic. However, afterwards, Mr. Jovanovic called some other people up and conveyed to them certain instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you did enter the office of President Cosic to deal with this matter concerning Mr. Gadhafi of Libya?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We waited for a long time until the connection was established, and then we went inside. Mr. Jovanovic and I, we went into Mr. Cosic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you, before I ask you what occurred inside that office, can you please describe where Mr. Cosic was sitting, where you were sitting, and where Mr. Jovanovic was sitting.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the table was the telephone. Mr. Cosic was to my right. I was sitting down, I was on his left, therefore. Across from Mr. Cosic was Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you please describe what occurred in that room, and only describe the events regarding Mr. Gadhafi to the extent that they are relevant to this Chamber's inquiry.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Libyan leader had a very noble idea and asked the then-Yugoslav president, that is to say Mr. Dobrica Cosic, that all the leaders of the then-Yugoslavia should come to see him in Tripoli - he would send a special plane for them - and that they could negotiate a peaceful solution to the problems they had over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was the purpose of the discussion to make arrangements or negotiate regarding that matter or that offer?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. However, the important thing to stress here is that Mr. Cosic was not able to utter a single sentence to the Libyan leader. I had to translate everything that was said over the phone until Minister Jovanovic told him what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I correct in what you're describing, or understanding what you're describing, that when Mr. Gadhafi would say something to you on the phone, you would translate so that Mr. Cosic and Mr. Jovanovic could hear what you were translating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who was responsible for --

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was responsible for what was said back to Mr. Gadhafi during this telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was decided during that conversation by Minister Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who would -- and then who would then -- am I correct in thinking that you would then translate whatever was said back to Mr. Gadhafi?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the ultimate outcome? Was the offer by Mr. Gadhafi accepted or was it rejected?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offer of the leader Mr. Gadhafi was neither rejected nor accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After that phone conversation, what happened?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that phone conversation, Mr. Cosic asked everybody to leave his office, but he asked me to stay behind with him, alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have a conversation with Mr. Cosic regarding that telephone conversation and other matters?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was surprised. I was really surprised, because I had never met Mr. Cosic before personally at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please summarise that conversation that you had with Mr. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cosic asked me at the time to be his advisor, as he said, for Islamic questions, as he put it, both within Yugoslavia and in relations with the Arab and Islamic world. He asked me many things about Islamic tolerance and literally, among other things, he said the following: "I would really like to ask you, because I've heard a lot about you, that you're a great expert in Islamic questions, for you to be my advisor, to help me." And he said the following sentence quite literally: "It is untenable that our Slav Muslims, Sunits, should be killed so brutally. Please come and be my advisor. Help me to do something."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During his conversation with you, did he make any reference to his relationship with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and that happened in the following way: The conversation went on for quite some time, and I told Mr. Cosic on the occasion - and he managed to charm me, I must say, with the attitude he took - I said that I was one of those people from the generation who had taken great pleasure in reading the book. The book is called the Daleko Je Sunce, "Far is the Sun," about the anti-fascist struggle and everything, and from the book, and as I was meeting him for the first time, I was able to gather that this was a noble man who wanted to give meaning to his life. And then I said to President Cosic, each one of us wants to give meaning to their lives, to do good and prevent evil. And I said, "Mr. President, God has never given anyone a chance to give meaning to their lives as he has to you here today." And he was resigned and said, "What has God given me?" And I was so moved that I knelt down before the president and entreated him, "Please, save the Bosnian children. If you manage to save just one Bosnian child's life, you will have given meaning to your life." And then he whispered very sadly. He turned towards Dedinje Hill and he said: "How can I do that? You saw a moment ago I -- Despot Milosevic won't even allow me to open my mouth. I can't say anything. I'm just a puppet in his hands here. That is why I entreat you, be my advisor. I am trying to form, to set up a group of people, a group of experts in my cabinet, and I would like to try become independent, if I can. I have no authority here. I have been completely subjugated. You saw that a moment ago. Even this ordinary conversation with the Libyan leader I cannot conduct without being dictated to and told what to say."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ambassador, after this meeting with Mr. Cosic, did you ever have any future meetings with him regarding his proposal for you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was my last meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to a period later, around the time that Mr. Panic was made Prime Minister. Were you invited to a celebration of his inauguration as Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The service for which I still worked officially was invited. Among my colleagues, the men and women, I was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this celebration, would it have been after the fall of Vukovar and the events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I was surprised, because one of the people who greeted us in the White Palace, Beli Dvor, when we arrived at the reception, was Mr. Sljivancanin, and he gave us the impression that he was some sort of chief there, head of the employees in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic arrive or attend that celebration?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic did arrive later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was he there at the same time that Mr. Sljivancanin, or Colonel Sljivancanin, was present?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that because the celebrations took place in the park of the White Palace, its grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of that evening, did Colonel Sljivancanin make statements regarding what had occurred in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Sljivancanin sat at our table for a time, and he spoke about his so-called moves in Vukovar, how he bravely killed the enemy, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was he saying these statements privately or were they said in confidence or were they said publicly to the people at the table?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that publicly in front of all of us round that table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything else of importance that occurred at this during course of this evening?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was quite obvious that evening was that there was the diplomatic corps there, all the high-ranking officials of the federal state at the time, and of Serbia too, but it was quite obvious that Mr. Milosevic was the number one personage during the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what do you base that conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base that conclusion on the fact that when Mr. Milosevic appeared on the terrace of the White Palace, there was a round of applause. Some people applauded him and everyone in a way was happy to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you testified the day before yesterday that you remained in Belgrade up until 1994. If I could draw your attention to the fall of 1992, the period of time between the fall of 1992 and up until the time you left in 1994, did you ever have occasion to see the movement of Yugoslav army troops in and around the Belgrade area?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. During that period, the general situation in Belgrade was such that it was geared towards Bosnia and Croatia, and you could see convoys very often moving around town, military convoys crossing the bridges across the Sava River. Belgrade was full of different men in different uniforms belonging to different troops. Belgrade restaurants were full of them. You could see uniforms everywhere, especially at the beginning of 1992 and 1993. These people were excited, talking about their so-called war feats in Bosnia, Croatia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If troops were to move from Belgrade to Bosnia, would they have to cross the bridges over the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely right. All roads led from Belgrade across the Sava River bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the next topic I would ask you to deal with the Chamber has heard some evidence about concerning media reports. Can I ask you to summarise briefly what you recall about the media reports that you saw while living in Belgrade during this time period?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Belgrade for all of us, that is to say non-Serbs and for all free-thinking Serbs who were not -- did not think like Mr. Milosevic, the situation was very difficult. In a difficult situation of this kind, the media gave their incredible contribution, both the written media, that is to say the press, and the electronic media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to describe just generally the types of media accounts that you saw, that you believed to be being used in this manner.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in the written press but in the electronic media, especially television played its key role, and almost every night on television you would have programmes talking about the fact that all other nations were genocidal and it was only the Serbs that were threatened and jeopardised during that time, that they should return their dignity. It was all fabricated and rigged. And let me say that one evening there was a particular programme which said that the Muslims in Bosnia or, rather, the Bosnian army was raping only Serb women. And in that programme there were several so-called experts who had been called in to appear, doctors, professors and others, and there was a woman there and she spoke in the Bosnian dialect, and her -- her back was turned to the camera and you could deduce that she was a pregnant woman, you could just see her silhouette. There were similar programmes every night, but in this particular one, the lady said that she had been raped repeatedly in Bosnia, somewhere around Tuzla, and as she said, Alija's soldiers were terribly brutal towards her, she called them, towards her and the other ladies who were there. They were terribly brutal until she became pregnant, finally. Once she became pregnant, they behaved quite differently and decently. And then they asked her to go -- to move to the territory which was under Serb control. She asked them. And the experts in the programme taking part explained about why that was so, why that happened. I think that it was Doctor Professor Vlado Vojvodic. I don't know exactly, but I know that he introduced himself as being a doctor and a professor and a specialist from the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade, and he said to the letter the following sentence: "I'm not only a doctor and specialist for such-and-such, I am at the same time, and many people won't know this, an expert for Islamic studies. I'm an Islamologist. And everything that our patient said a moment ago is true, because in their genocidal book the Koran, it says --" and he quoted the paragraph, the sentence that he was referring to about -- it says, "Muslims, rape the infidels whenever you have a chance to do so, especially Serb women. Rape them and be brutal towards them until one of them becomes pregnant."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ambassador, if I could now draw your attention to another topic, are you familiar with a person by the name of Milanko Renovica?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know the person. I know Mr. Milanko Renovica. Mr. Milanko Renovica was at one time a high-ranking official in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was also president of the Presidency and party president as well, and I would often have occasion to see him while he was holding his post in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At one time he had a position in Belgrade. I don't know which one, but I think a high-ranking Yugoslav party function it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm more interested at this time in did you ever have occasion to overhear a conversation that he was having in a restaurant that you were also present in regarding events in Foca?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When -- when, to the best of your recollection --

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- was this conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation, as far as I can recollect now, took place in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you summarise that conversation, as best you recall it.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place in the restaurant of the Palace Hotel in Belgrade. I was having dinner of an evening with two of my friends. The restaurant that night was full to capacity, and most of the people there, as it wasn't a large restaurant, as far as I was able to see, came from Bosnia. All of them had large quantities of food and the most expensive drinks out on their tables, and in -- at one of the next door tables was Milanko Renovica. I feared that he might recognise me and I tried as much as possible to have my back towards him. At Milanko Renovica's table, I heard some very -- some stories that I could barely stomach at the time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Everybody bragged about that. They bragged about, boasted about what they had done in Foca. And finally, they summarised and said the following: "It's not important how many balijas were there, Muslims there. The important thing is that there'll never be any of them there again."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last topic I would ask you to deal with is the following: You are a member of the Muslim faith, are you not?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time period, did you attend a mosque in Belgrade? During the time you were living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am of Muslim faith, but I'm proud of the multi-cultural Bosnia and Herzegovina. In those days, I did go occasionally, because the situation was so difficult, and it was the only place where all of us who happened to be in Belgrade found ourselves in an intolerable, humiliating situation. We went there perhaps to find a way of doing something for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to tell us the name of the mosque and the neighbourhood in Belgrade where it is situated.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is easy because it is the only remaining mosque in Belgrade. It's a small one. It's called Bajrakli dzamija. It's at the end of Knez Mihajlova Street, towards Kalemegdan Park to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you would go to the mosque, were you ever videotaped entering the mosque?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almost regularly all of us who gathered there in fear were exposed to regular filming by the official TV station of Serbia. The cameraman would zoom on each individual, from one face to another, so that each face was registered. And this would also happen during prayers. I remember once that the Belgrade imam was interrupted, and he was unable to contain himself, but he told the cameraman on whose camera the word Filipovic was written, he said, "Sir, will you please stop filming us? You're filming not just our faces but also our shoes. Finish your job so we can start our prayers." The cameraman answered arrogantly, "Everyone's doing his job. I am on assignment here."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time when the mosque came under attack?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While I was still in Belgrade, the mosque was attacked twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you please summarise the severity of the attack and the general circumstances surrounding those two attacks.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those attacks, as far as I can remember, took place at night, and I am convinced that the aim of those attacks was to increase fear and terror among the Muslims so that they would leave Belgrade. I remember on Fridays when I would go to the mosque many faces were missing. People left or either they were afraid to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to describe the attacks in greater detail. What type of attacks; what was used, if you know; what damage was done, if you know.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were attacks with grenades, as far as I can remember. Hand grenades were thrown in. And the external part of the mosque was partially damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, when did these attacks occur?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- one attack was in 1992. Then there was another one. I don't know whether it was at the end of the 1992 or the beginning of 1993, but I'm sure that there were two attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with a member of the mosque regarding his attempts to seek protection for the mosque from Mr. Milosevic after these attacks?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to the Belgrade mufti. His name is Mr. Hamdija Jusuf-Spahic. He understood the situation of dreadful terror that all of us were exposed to in Belgrade, and he tried to flirt with Mr. Milosevic, using the slogans of protecting Yugoslavia, et cetera. And he kept asking Mr. Milosevic to receive him so that he could protect the Muslims who were frightened to death. However, as far as I know, Mr. Milosevic never wanted to receive Mr. Jusuf-Spahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would Mr. Jusuf-Spahic have been one of the most prominent members of the Muslim community living in Belgrade, or even in Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. He was the Belgrade mufti. He was the leading figure for all Muslims in the whole of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that I don't forget, because this is not in the statement, and I was told that Mr. Groome would examine him very briefly ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, at the end you spoke about the attacks on the Bajrakli mosque. First you said it was the only remaining mosque in Belgrade. Did anyone destroy any mosques in Belgrade so this was the remaining one when you use that expression?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. When the Turks withdrew from Belgrade in 1846, there were 364 mosques in Belgrade. All of them were destroyed, and only this Bajrakli one remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were those mosques destroyed except for this one that was left standing?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the Turks left. And I don't think that is the subject of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is, because you've said it was the only remaining one. So the impression one has is that we had destroyed some mosques. There were no other mosques even before I was born and before you were born as far as I know too. Was a single mosque in Belgrade destroyed in Belgrade or in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, Mr. Milosevic, all of them were destroyed. After the Turks left, after the Turks left and the persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the nineteenth century, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I will remind you, Mr. Milosevic, that there were more than 12.000 Muslims in Belgrade and this small remaining mosque and I underlining "remaining," could certainly not satisfy the needs of the faithful. But your authorities would never allow a new mosque to be built. And I was a witness when the Libyan leader, Gadhafi, as you've asked me let me remind you, I think it was in 1996, had agreed with the then-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia at the time. I was a witnessed at that; I interpreted on that occasion. Mr. Petar Stambolic was the president at the time. The visit occurred on a Friday, the day of prayers, and he officially accompanied Mr. Gadhafi to this small Belgrade mosque, and he said, "Let me build you a mosque, let me assist you." Because people were praying in the street because the mosque is small. But you would never allow Gadhafi or anyone else to build a new mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did I have to do with any of that in 1986, with anything, permissions for the building of a garage, never find a mosque.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you never wanted to receive the mufti. Among other things, he wanted to complain about not allowing a mosque to be built.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the untruths among many that you have uttered. I received Mr. Hamdija Jusuf-Spahic innumerable times, and I consider him to be an honourable man. Maybe I overdid it when I said innumerable times, but certainly many times. Secondly, do you know, since I see you worked in the federal government, that there wasn't a single official reception in Serbia that among other religious leaders that were invited to attend that Mr. Jusuf-Spahic was not invited to? Was there a single formal occasion, any celebration by the city of Belgrade, the state of Serbia or the state of Yugoslavia that Mr. Jusuf-Spahic was not invited to? I met him on many occasions. On those occasion and also on others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the question. What he's put is that in fact this gentleman was asked to receptions in Belgrade and by the federal government. Can you help about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that he was invited, but Mr. Jusuf-Spahic on, endless occasions, told me that Mr. Milosevic never wanted to receive him officially. At all official receptions, Mr. Jusuf-Spahic begged to be allowed to make a new mosque, but he was never given permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic. I'm not just saying how many times I met Mr. Jusuf-Spahic, exchanged greetings, shook hands with him at official occasion, but I'm also saying that he came to my office on several occasions. He asked to be received and was received. But you obviously don't know that. You're saying that none of this is true?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one thing to shake hands with someone and it's something else to receive him in official audience and hear his requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said both.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the conversations I had with Mr. Jusuf-Spahic, and I had them frequently, I never understood that you did him the honour of receiving him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you now I did receive him several times. Secondly, you know that only an irresponsible person, obviously a criminal, threw a hand grenade into the yard of the mosque and that after that, the police guarded the mosque.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at the same time, your TV filmed each of our faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I think really there's no point in making such assertions because the TV films liturgies in the palace church in Belgrade and the faces of people attending those liturgies. When the patriarch is giving a sermon or a bishop, this is frequently filmed and shown on television. So why is this a question of importance? Surely the media are free. Are they nod allowed to film these things? We see them filming liturgies in Jerusalem, on various masses that are being filmed on television?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that liturgies and masses are filmed and broadcast, but in this case there was only filming and not broadcasting. I think Mr. Jusuf-Spahic provided an answer when, with resignation, he appealed to the cameraman to allow him to continue the prayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The patriarch, His Holiness Mr. Pavle could also tell the cameraman to move out, if he's nervous, if he's being bothered by his presence. But let us not waste any more time on this point. Did you, for instance, see on television when there's a formal service in the mosque in Belgrade on the occasion of Bajram or some other religious holiday? Then there's a short feature. Of course, the cameraman films a longer period, but then a short report appears in the news that there was a celebration of such-and-such an event. Did you see that on television?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only on Montenegrin television and only when Montenegro managed to get rid of you, at least to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you never saw that on Belgrade television, that Muslim believers are celebrating their holiday? You never saw that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your time that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic, very well. That's fine. Now, tell me, do you at least remember that after that incident when someone threw in a hand grenade into the mosque yard nobody was hurt and no serious damage was done, that the police guarded the mosque to prevent any such thing from happening again, because it was assumed that this was someone irresponsible, someone among those who had fled from the areas where they had been subjected to the terror of Muslim forces had done it and they had sought shelter in Belgrade and had found it?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade at the time was full of - what do you call them - paramilitaries under your direct control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic. I never had any paramilitaries, but that is not the subject of your testimony. We will leave that to the opposing side. Do you know that the police took care of not just the Bajrakli mosque in Belgrade but made sure that not a single mosque in Serbia should be damaged and that not a single one was damaged?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I said that the Belgrade mosque was damaged twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You referred to those two incidents.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the mosque was damaged twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the police guarded it.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it guarded it. If they had guarded it properly, the damage wouldn't have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic. During the war in Bosnia, was a single mosque destroyed in Serbia, a single one?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, let me not mention the suffering of Muslims under your control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether a single one was damaged.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was living in Belgrade. But I repeat that your police cared for the mosque so well that it was damaged or bombed twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when someone throws in a hand grenade at night into the yard that is bombing, that is bombardment?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The police carried out an investigation and then guarded it, making sure that it wouldn't happen again. No one was hurt. In fact, the state provided funds for it to be repaired and for other things to be done linked to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A separate point and then I think we've exhausted this particular topic. Mr. Pasic, can you help us, were funds provided for the repair, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For repairing the mosque do you mean, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's what's being alleged.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, funds were never provided by Mr. Milosevic. They were collected by the faithful themselves. And as far as they were able, they renovated and repaired their facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the state never provided any money for the repairs of the mosque in Belgrade. That is what you are asserting; is that right? Very well. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the only Belgrade mosque ever received anything from you. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't need to know that, but you know other things which you really couldn't -- you couldn't have known. Anyway, since we have established that not a single mosque in Belgrade was destroyed, not a single one throughout that time, did any Muslim, because he was a Muslim, was he arrested or killed in Serbia during the whole period of the war in Bosnia? Do you know perhaps about that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us who were living --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were all killed, were you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under your rule of terror, Mr. Milosevic, exchanged greetings in whispers, saying to one another, "How is your yellow band doing?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why? Were you wearing a yellow ribbon around your shoulders?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how we felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are claiming that is how you felt?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All your broadcasts in all your media representing the Muslims as genocidal resulted in this horrific condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely this horrific condition was brought about by the behaviour of Islamic extremists in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the horrific atrocities they committed against the Serbs in those days, Mr. Pasic, and not what you call my television.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you were the stage manager of everything, of the horrific ethnic cleansing due to which you are sitting where you're sitting, started from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I know very well why I am sitting in this chair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to have this sort of argument, and it's no point personalising it. Find some other topic, Mr. Milosevic, than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned -- it's not in your statement but you mentioned Milanko Renovica and, yes, he was a politician from Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was also president of the Presidency of the Central Committee and he occupied the top posts in Yugoslavia. At the beginning of those conflicts, he withdrew from political life completely. Nobody ever heard of him throughout the war. The man was quite passive. So how come now you ascribe to Milanko Renovica some kind of Serb nationalism?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that Mr. Renovica was not a nationalist. He wouldn't sit around in the restaurant of the Palace Hotel with people like that. And as far as I was informed, Mr. Renovica was sort of a political advisor of some sort to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that, Mr. Pasic, things like that being said, but that was towards the end of the war. And as a pensioner, otherwise he lived in his weekend cottage in Sokolac where he originated from and he was completely passive throughout the war. But I did hear about that, that at the end of the war, as an experienced politician with many years of experience, the leadership of Republika Srpska did ask him to assist them with respect to certain -- to giving certain political advice, but that was right at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard, Mr. Milosevic. What I heard was that you ordered him to be an advisor to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Pasic. Judging by what you're saying, I was in charge of the television, I wrote the newspapers, I appointed counsellors and advisors to everyone.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely so. But let's move on. You spoke about the media, the nationalist programmes. Unfortunately, it is -- you will be -- you know that scripta remnant, verba volant, the Latin proverb "what is written remains" and we'll be able to go through all that, all the media. Those who were under state control or state influence, they in fact worked to calm the situation. So what you're saying is not true, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must ask questions rather than making statements, as you know quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you quoted an example from the media. You quoted programmes, broadcasts about a Serb woman who had been raped and was quite obviously pregnant. Well, is that a Serb crime maybe, that a Serb be raped, a Serb woman be raped by the Muslim side? And you are bringing that up as a crime committed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just quoted one of many examples put forward by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your television. The crime was what the media wanted to show, and the man said quite literally, he introduced himself as being professor and doctor, that in the Koran it said that the infidel women should be raped until they become pregnant, and once they become pregnant behave decently towards them because the child that is going to be born will be a Mujahedin, which means that this is a pladjijet [phoen]. And you wanted -- instead of preventing unbelievable broadcasts of that kind --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that there was a programme like that. And secondly, tell me what the Koran does indeed say about that. I haven't read that paragraph of the Koran, but perhaps you could tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting a very long way from the subject matter of this case, and this kind of argument does not assist the Trial Chamber. Now, find something else to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll ask him about other things, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Sljivancanin. In your statement, you wrote -- you wrote: "I saw Sljivancanin in the White Palace. He was a great hero and boasted about how he had destroyed Vukovar," which is quite unbelievable. And then you say: "He said that he had been given this post by Milosevic, whom he referred to as the Commander-in-Chief." Now, please, Mr. Pasic, we have to have -- you can't falsify material facts. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find out first of all whether what is alleged is true. Did Sljivancanin say that he had been given a post by Milosevic who he referred to as the Commander-in-Chief? Now, did that happen, Mr. Pasic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sljivancanin, at the time, really did speak about those feats of his. And when Mr. Milosevic appeared on the balcony of the White Palace, he got up, saluted him in military fashion, and later on he said that Mr. Milosevic was the greatest leader that the Serbs ever had and that he would quite certainly preserve this great state and that we could quite obviously -- you could deduce that Mr. Sljivancanin saw Mr. Milosevic as being his Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You deduced this. And was it only Sljivancanin who got up when I came in or did you all get up? Perhaps you yourself didn't get to your feet.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that everybody got up to their feet.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if you all got up, why did you single out Sljivancanin from all those many people?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Sljivancanin had a smiling face and turned towards you and saluted you as you would a military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. That was your deduction, was it? Now, you say -- now, do you know that Sljivancanin was, as far as I know, assistant commander of the Guards Brigade for security, or chief of the department - I don't know how this was defined - of the Guards Brigade. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you best know how you deployed your commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, that was at the time when I had no jurisdiction over the JNA, and Mr. Sljivancanin was in the Guards Brigade. He was there before I ever became president, and the Guards Brigade precisely has the function of providing security for the leadership of the SFRY or the FRY, whichever you like, so he was performing his job, and that's how he came to be there, not in any other capacity.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's interesting that I never saw Mr. Sljivancanin there before, and he occupied that post even before. I saw him only after those, in inverted commas, courageous feats of his in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Pasic. I don't want to dwell on that any further, but as you yourself have just confirmed what you wrote in your statement, that's not true, and I have to listen to stupid things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. Mr. Sljivancanin found himself in the White Palace for the first time after those feats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the Guards Brigade provide security for the White Palace and its grounds, and Sljivancanin had to provide security. And in 1989 and 1990, and 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why wasn't he ever there before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How should I know that whether he was there or not? Were you always there, in the White Palace, to see who was coming and going?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've had sufficient of this argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I think you didn't answer to the question whether Mr. Sljivancanin had said that he had been given a post by Mr. Milosevic, who he referred to as the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He spoke about Mr. Milosevic with admiration, and he would speak at length of how he went to war in Croatia and so on, and he saw Mr. Milosevic as a Supreme Commander. And he said at one point that Mr. Milosevic had appointed him to be some kind of maitre d' or the main host in the White Palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, that reception was organised by the organisers of the federation. You don't suppose that I dealt with matters of protocol in the federation. How can you claim that at all?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you probably rewarded some of the warriors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there's any point in me asking you anything else about that. You've gone beyond anything of good taste and style. Tell me please, Mr. Pasic, you're a Muslim yourself, as you've said, who until 1994 worked in the government, in the SFRY and later on in the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's right, isn't it? Until 1994; isn't that right, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as far as I can see, nobody dismissed you from your job, did they, in the post you occupied, either before 1994 or in 1994. Isn't that right, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all those services, federal services, of Yugoslavia at the time when you came into power was purged of all those who did not agree with your concepts. So not only the non-Serbs but the Serbs too who didn't support you whole-heartedly. They had to leave too, step down from these organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, there's no point in telling untruths of that kind. Would you please just limit your answers to answering my questions. What I asked you was this: Nobody dismissed you from the job you have occupied before 1994 or in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, just answer my questions, and if you want to make a statement, you can ask the Trial Chamber to allow you to make a statement, but it is your duty to answer my questions. Is it true that in 1994, as you yourself say in your statement on page 4, paragraph 7, that you fled from Belgrade, from Yugoslavia, and went to Hungary?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then from thence you went on to Cairo?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why did you flee from Yugoslavia? Tell me that. Why did you escape?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In formal terms, I stayed on in my job. You read my statement. I was demoted; nobody gave me any work to do, I didn't have any work to do. You read in my statement that I was protected too by a highly-positioned friend at the time, and had it not been for him, God knows what would have happened to me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I don't know what God knows and what God knows would have happened to you, but tell me this: In Yugoslavia at that time until you had fled, as you say, were you prosecuted in any way? Was any lawsuit brought against you or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. No lawsuit was ever brought against me, no criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you have any private problems for which you say you had to flee Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. I was exposed many times to unpleasantnesses of various kinds and threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you can fabricate and invent things of that kind elsewhere but not here. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, you can't put allegations like that. If you want to suggest that the witness is fabricating, you can, but you can't put a generalisation of that sort. Are you suggesting that he's fabricating that he was subjected to threats?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Well, he worked in the federal organs in 1994 and then he got into some vehicle of some kind and drove off to Hungary quite freely, without any -- without any obstacles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had a good time of it, why would I have had to flee?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you had other ambitions, Mr. Pasic, but I don't want to delve into that now. Tell me this, please: Did any organ ever take away your travelling documents?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was controlled and supervised all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Pasic. That means you had your passport, and the most lenient measure -- the first measure to bear out what you are saying when you said that they wouldn't allow you to go -- to leave with your secrets, that's what you started off by saying, well, the least thing they would have done was to ask you to return your passport. And they didn't take your passport away. So, Mr. Pasic, my question to you is this: Why do you say you escaped when you normally got into a vehicle of some kind with a passport in your pocket, you passed the border crossing quite normally, went through customs control and passport control and nobody detained you and you just drove off into Hungary?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I worked in Belgrade for a long time, as chance would have it, until you came to power, and I really did feel quite civilised there. I lived a civilised life. But after you arrived, after your advent, luckily I had friends because there were honourable people in your institutions too, and they provided me with protection and they assisted me, Mr. Milosevic, and helped me not have my passport taken away from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let us clarify. What was it that you fled from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fled from unbearable degradation and terror that we all lived through in Belgrade. It wasn't only I myself who fled but honourable Serbs left the country too. Mr. Bogdan Bogdanovic, a case in point. He left. He couldn't take it any more. And many other honourable Serbs. I felt at the time just like any Jew would have felt in 1941 or 1942 in Berlin. I didn't feel -- I felt -- that's how I felt. I didn't feel in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just establish the facts, Mr. Pasic. You claimed during the examination-in-chief that allegedly the representatives of the police said that they wouldn't allow you, wouldn't permit you to leave, and we have taken note that nobody took away your travel documents and that you crossed the border quite legally. You showed your passport, you passed through the passport and customs control, and as you know, at the passport control they always have a list of persons blacklisted, people who they keep back. You were not on the list, I'm sure, because you were allowed to pass across the border. So why did you say you fled? You just travelled to Budapest.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, there were honourable Serbs, friends of mine who provided protection. And then in certain villages they even provided accommodation for me had I needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Pasic. We have established the facts and can now move on. If it was the way -- if things were the way you say they were, that times were difficult in the way you describe them, I was president as of 1989, you were leaving Belgrade quite legally with a passport in your pocket and you were travelling to Budapest, why didn't you leave Belgrade before that? Why did it take you five years? You lived under those conditions in which you say you felt like a Jew in 1941 and 1942. Why did you stay there for five years?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I -- you know full well, Mr. Milosevic, that Belgrade was full of people loyal to you, servants to you, members of Arkan's formations, Seselj's men. At every bus stop in Belgrade, you would see proclamations asking people to call up for training, young men to be trained. And many people who attempted to leave Belgrade before me had some unpleasantness. Some people even committed suicide. At least, that's what your press reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about now, who committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll explain what I mean, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, explain. I don't understand what you're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My very dear colleague, a man I used to work with, was the late Mr. Zeljko Biserko, and he managed to escape to Hungary before me, that same country. I don't know, but your press wrote at the time that he committed suicide after he had escaped to Hungary. And the people who controlled him told me very often, "You mustn't leave without our knowledge, because what self- -- because suicide could befall you too."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, were that true, wouldn't they have just taken your passport away from you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you that I had amongst those people too people who respected me as I did them. They were my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic. In any event, the facts say that not a single official organ provided any obstacles, that you were not fired in 1994 but that you left normally and legally to Budapest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have now exhausted this topic. We have been over it many times. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in 1991, you were demoted to the lowest position of apprentice and that you had nothing -- nothing was given you to do.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not apprentice but the initial level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a reorganisation in the service or something? Or maybe I engaged in the organisation of the administration in the federal government.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you didn't, but your men did. Mr. Cosic couldn't open his mouth without your orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really surprised that you're speaking in such a humiliating manner about Mr. Cosic. But Mr. Cosic is alive, and I assume it's not a problem for him to confirm or deny such allegations on your part. I think it is really in bad taste for you to speak in that way about Mr. Cosic.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not speaking about Mr. Cosic without respect, Mr. Milosevic, but if there is a humiliating position, then it was Mr. Cosic's position, and you were the cause of it. He told me that himself. That's why he wanted me to be his advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really intrigued. You say that Mr. Cosic offered you the post of advisor. Why didn't you accept to be his advisor?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could never accept that for moral reasons. If Mr. Cosic was your puppet, then logically his advisors would be that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, surely set yourself some limits. Mr. Cosic is a proud man. It is really in bad taste to describe him as my puppet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about bad taste. This is what the witness said happened. Now, you can challenge it if you want. There's no point arguing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm not arguing at all. I think it is in bad taste for this witness to insult in that way a person such as Dobrica Cosic. It is really in bad taste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, it doesn't matter about the taste. It's the evidence we're interested in here and we're concerned with, and it's what the witness said happened. Now, you can challenge it, as I've said, but that is the evidence. It doesn't matter about the taste or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To insult people is certainly in bad taste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at least in the period you were referring to, you were not working in the Foreign Ministry but you were in the translation service of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the federal Executive Council or the federal organs; it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite remember who was my superior because I said I was demoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, who replaced you from the position of head of section that you say you headed?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like many, the plan was for me to be fired from that service, but one of my friends who had power in spite of your reign of terror kept me in that starting position because that was the only way that he could protect me and my frightened family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, we have established that no one fired you in 1992 or in 1994 when you left Belgrade in a legal manner which you yourself are not denying. Now, who is the person who replaced you? How can you not remember that somebody demoted you? Who is that person who was your immediate superior and who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all federal bodies, detailed purges were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the name of your superior who signed a decision whereby you're being appointed to another position.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go over this again. He says he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that every Monday you went to the MUP of Serbia for an interview.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the federal organs, yet I went to the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that some people raided your apartment.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone searching your apartment?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the results of such searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So somebody secretly, when you were not in the apartment, broke in and searched it.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some people from your services would come. They were always in plain clothes. They never introduced themselves. They would enter the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. apartment while we were inside, my family and me, and they took away a number of my books which they considered to be -- considered fundamentalist material because they were in the Hebrew, Persian, or Arabic languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic. Since you were an official or, rather, an employee of the federal organs, therefore, you were aware of your civil rights. Do you have any certificate for the property seized from you, any kind of certificate or instructions for research that needed to be provided if this were true?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you in 1941 ask for any kind of certificate in Berlin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you know very well there was no violence. You yourself couldn't mention a single person that was victimised. Therefore, it's really taking things too far to compare this with Berlin and the Jews. You were a citizen of Yugoslavia, and no one could enter your apartment without a warrant, and no one could seize your property without giving you a receipt. Do you know that, Mr. Pasic? And why are you making things up like that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Accused, I am not making up anything. I'm just presenting facts. I was a citizen of your then-state but without any rights, totally disenfranchised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find this out. You say your flat was entered. How many days did that happen, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know exactly how many times. It happened very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, Mr. Pasic, do you know that in the time when the Muslims, as you say, were discriminated against in Serbia, do you know how many Muslims there were in the army, in the police, in the state security, in the military security, in all the structures? Do you know how many Muslims there were? From the level of general in the army to I don't know which rank or member of the police force or police station commander or -- do you know how many Muslims there were holding those positions when you personally were discriminated against? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know, Mr. Milosevic, is as I said a moment ago and I claim that the ethnic cleansing started out from Belgrade. You cleansed not only all the organs of non-Serbs but also disobedient Serbs had to be moved away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We've already heard that. I really don't know who in Serbia was involved with any activities in the federal organs, but what you're saying is not true.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you own a single piece of paper, a formal decision regarding your moving to a different post or the search of your apartment or your interviews, information interviews, or any legal act that you claim was engaged in or, rather, against you? Do you have any evidence, any receipt, any document that would corroborate what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But your system functioned illegally. I don't have any document. I probably have the decision whereby I was demoted, but otherwise I never received any written documents regarding searches or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You even say that your wife suspected that you had a mistress. How come your wife didn't know that every Monday at 10.00 you had to go for this informative interview?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed my wife about that only once we reached Cairo, because I was clearly told that I mustn't tell anyone ever about any of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But since you had to act in such a conspiratorial manner, which are those secrets that you knew, that deserved such conspiracy and that intrigued those people so much? What are those secrets? Tell us here. What are the secrets that you had the key to? And you were not even allowed to talk about them with your wife.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I was fully conscious of everything in those days. I wouldn't let anyone say anything bad about you, especially on the phone because I was aware of the condition I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, because you say you were the subject of attention because of certain secrets. Which of those secrets that they were interested in?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can ask them. You know that until you came, I was involved in all the confidential talks at the highest political, economic, military levels, and probably that is what they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So they assumed that you were familiar with the content of the talks that you interpreted. So what? Then every interpreter, according to that criterion, is an object of security interest. Maybe these here too, because there are protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but their houses are not being searched and they're not invited for interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, these sort of generalisations are of no assistance. Mr. Milosevic, you have until the adjournment with this witness if you require it. The Prosecution had under three-quarters of an hour. You will have had 55 minutes or so which is, in our judgement, more than enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more will I have after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You will have until the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the break is in five minutes, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what to ask then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you went for an interview to the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, can you give us the names of the people who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which interview you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Any of those interviews that you had in the ministry in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever gave me a name, and of course I never asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pasic. On page 2, paragraph 3, you claim that the leaders of the Arab world in 1992, 1993, usually had contacts with me. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who were those leaders that had dealings with me?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course fortunately I never had access to your office, and I was never invited to such talks, but in the Arab -- you know who supported you among the Arab countries in those days, and who sent you special messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am expecting you to give that answer, because that is what you are claiming and not me.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is common knowledge, it is nothing confidential. You had very close relations with Saddam, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I had close relations with Saddam?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, please, since you are explaining this, who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. It was known. Oh, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from some people that I was friends with, with any comments who were close to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who, for instance?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people. I'd rather not mention them for their benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please give us the names. If necessary, we can go into private session, because you are making up everything. It is quite unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't made up anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have made up everything, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is how we waste time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that in the waiting room of Mr. Cosic, you saw at the same time some muddied soldiers, Martic, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs Jovanovic, and I don't know who else. So while you were there. And you heard all kinds of conversations, and then now in this oral examination you explained -- you explained here that Zlatko Jovanovic said to me, "Mr. Slobo," and "Mr. President." You said this, you can find this in the transcript. Tell me just once again, how did he address me?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, these were just bits and pieces that I heard. Of course I didn't hear all the orders you gave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But how did he address me?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "President Slobo."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say here in your statement that you signed the collocutor was addressed with the words, "Comrade Slobo," "Comrade President, and Slobodan Milosevic was then president of Serbia." Of course, that is not in dispute; in 1992 I was president of Serbia. Do you know that he never addressed me by name, Mr. Jovanovic, and never with the word "comrade." He never used that term, but exclusively with the term "Mr. President." Therefore, when are you telling the truth, Mr. Pasic, here in the statement, or now when you're explaining things, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. First of all, he's given his evidence. That's what he heard the man say. You dispute that. Did he refer to the -- did Jovanovic refer to the accused as "Comrade President" or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Jovanovic addressed him with "President." I'm quite sure, and I stand by what I wrote and what I said, that Jovanovic spoke directly to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's another question. That's another matter.
