I'm just denying something that is unbelievable in the form of address, which is also an indication that other things are unbelievable. A moment ago, Mr. Pasic, you said that he said not to worry and that Buha, Aleksa Buha, who was the Foreign Minister of Republika Srpska would not take the microphone again.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is quite so is it? Now let me tell you what you said in your statement. "Don't worry, Comrade Slobo. Leave that to me. I'll see to it that Radovan Karadzic doesn't get in front of a microphone again." So you can't even remember in this statement of three pages what you wrote, you couldn't remember that now that you are giving your oral testimony. You can't remember whether you wrote down Buha or Karadzic or what.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, talking to you, Mr. Milosevic, mentioned both. I wasn't so close to be able to register exactly everything, but what I did register is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in quotation marks, you say, "Don't worry, Comrade Slobo --" he never used the familiar term with me -- "I will see to it that Radovan Karadzic doesn't get in front of a microphone again." So this time you didn't remember Karadzic but you remembered Buha and you construed a completely different story here in the examination in relation to what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with the microphone, you mentioned both, both Karadzic and Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then later on you say that in that conversation, Goran Hadzic and Aleksa Buha were mentioned. "Milosevic was giving instructions." So he goes over there to see Cosic and then, using the telephone of Cosic's office, I give him instructions as to what he should do with Cosic, and he's the federal Minister of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same thing happened in Mr. Cosic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened? Perhaps I spoke to him while you were speaking to Gadhafi? Maybe I was speaking to Jovanovic and then he was passing on to Cosic what he thought?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Cosic complained about that. He was very sad. He was speaking in whispers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said that he was a puppet in my hands? You, like me, know the building and we know that the office of the president of the republic faces the Danube. So he couldn't have turned around towards Dedinje and faced Dedinje in his office. So you made even such a stupid detail up which any ordinary -- knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop the speech. This has been challenged. Which direction he turned may be of no significance at all, but whether the conversation took place or not is of significance. Now, the accused is alleging this conversation didn't take place on the phone, the conversation with Cosic. Is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not claiming that Cosic didn't speak to Gadhafi. He probably did, though I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The conversation with the witness is the one that's under -- now, can you answer that, please, Mr. Pasic, for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. The president of federal Yugoslavia at the time, Mr. Dobrica Cosic, was resigned. He was sad when I asked him to save at least a single Bosnian child, in a rather emotional conversation. Then he turned around, and in his large office in which you too worked you can face the Danube or Dedinje; it's very simple. He pointed in the direction of Dedinje and said, "You saw a moment ago that I can't even open my mouth. I can't say anything or do anything. That despot Milosevic is holding everything in his hands, he's the absolute master of everything, so please be my advisor." I'm trying. And he mentioned the names of some other people that he planned to appoint to other posts. "Help me in my office to try as much as I can to become independent of that despot." That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you assume that the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could come to a talk that Cosic is having with Gadhafi without the invitation of President Cosic? Could he have imposed his presence there? Could he enter his office at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You ask him. It's no good asking the witness. This is what the witness said happened. So it's no good asking him why Jovanovic was there or not. In any event, it's well past the time. You've had way over the time. You should know by now in cross-examination if you waste time on peripheral issues and arguing with the witness, it means that your time will be limited. And we're not having a case in which you argue and waste time endlessly with unimportant matters and then you complain that your time is limited. You ought to know by now it will be. Now, we'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I be given just five more minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just give me brief answers. How long did you live in Belgrade for?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen or 16 years in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sixteen years, right. How many times did you go to Bajrakli mosque?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times but a few times I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Five times, ten times, a rough idea?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I can't tell you how many times I went to the mosque but a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Sixteen years you lived went to Belgrade and you went a few times. You said you went to Bajrakli dzamija a number of times and you claimed that it was in Knez Mihajlova Street.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the district is called; I left Belgrade. But I described where Bajrakli dzamija is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said Knez Mihajlova Street by Kalemegdan Park.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I said when you walked down Knez Mihajlova Street, I said before you enter Kalemegdan Park, on the right-hand side is where there's a petrol pump, and in a little street there is where Bajrakli mosque is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, well, Bajrakli mosque is in Jevremova Street. You never went to Bajrakli dzamija, Mr. Pasic, I put it to you.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this then now, please. As you said that the people you were in the waiting-room with that they were all waiting some soldiers and others, and you say you think you saw Martic there too.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. You know what those corridors are like. I didn't say that I was sure it was him but people were carrying papers of some kind. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So Martic was waiting and these people were waiting to be received by Cosic, and Cosic spent two hours with you after talking to Gadhafi because he has nothing else to do, no better business; right?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many people were in the large cabinet of yours and in the offices around it and how many people were in the waiting rooms, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you say that you -- that I know the corridors well, you say that it was dark and that you were therefore not able to establish the insignia worn by these men in uniforms. You know full well that those corridors are very, very well lit. They're very broad corridors, very well lit and anybody ever entering the building knows that too.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't have time, nor did I have a chance to look at the details with respect to the insignia. But I'm certain that the insignia were as I described them, the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what were these markings of the brigade, Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago and, Mr. Milosevic, you would know that better than me. It was a very nice uniform and on the right hand there was an emblem which said "brigade" in the Cyrillic script, I think of the Ilidza Brigade. I'm almost 90 per cent certain that it was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, 90 per cent. You said that you weren't able to see exactly because of the dark corridor?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not because of the dark corridor alone. I was conscious of your men standing in every nook and cranny. So I was careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that when you were in the federal government building, you would see Krajisnik, Karadzic, Plavsic and the others there quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially at the beginning. Those people moved around there freely they were going to and from meetings. Who they went to see, where they went, I didn't know that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see me in that government building, for instance?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were these people going? Who were they going to see?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know. I said it a moment ago. You should know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, I should know who somebody is going to see in the government building on the other side of the Sava River. All right. Now tell me this. Why didn't you tell the investigators that before or, rather, once you left Belgrade before you reached Cairo, you spent some time in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't spend some time in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then tell me since when have you been Ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina? When did you become Bosnia-Herzegovina in Cairo?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Cairo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Kuwait then?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my third year in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who appointed you ambassador to Kuwait?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is the subject of our examination here, but I was appointed by the representative of my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who signed your credentials?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina appointed me ambassador, the Presidency did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't assume the whole Presidency signed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I don't think there's any relevance in this. You can ask one more question, Mr. Milosevic, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that it wasn't Alija Izetbegovic who signed your appointment papers?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of my country harmonises and coordinates the appointment of each and every ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the signature. Whose signature?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the signature the signature of Alija Izetbegovic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you read the Islamic declaration of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go into all that. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try and be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, could you please explain to us or, rather, to Their Honours why, in your statement that you gave to the investigators on the 6th, 7th and 10th of July, 2002, you did not refer to the fact that in the conversation with you, Dobrica Cosic had to whisper and that that was the occasion he spoke about himself as being part of a -- as a puppet. Why didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I compiled the statement last year, I gave the briefest possible passages from that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would not ask you my next question had you not mention two things here during the examination-in-chief and that is why I think I can ask you to explain some things to the Court in that regard. You mentioned a book, "Far Is the Sun," written by Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was his first book; right? If you don't know it doesn't matter, but do you know this: Immediately after that book was published, he published another book called "Deobe," "Divisions," in which he wrote in the most critical point -- critical way of Serb shortcomings and why after World War II, this book that dealt with Serb shortcomings was published so -- such a long time afterwards?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the book. I'm just telling you about the book I did read and the book we mentioned, Mr. Cosic and I, in our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that his books later on, some other books written by him later on disclosed the anomalies of the communist system, do you know about that, unmasked them?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Mr. Cosic and I had a long conversation, he said, when he asked me to be his advisor, he said this: "My books -- I have a lot of money and my books are selling like hotcakes."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about that. I was asking you did you need moral courage to publish books of that sort?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his books there is a lot of Serb nationalism, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that he was one of the first people to resist and stand up to the system that ruled under the reign of Josip Broz Tito? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was an opposition man, in the opposition, and I know also that he said that Mr. Milosevic was a despot, as I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. I asked you whether he was one of the first people to pluck up the courage to resist what was done during Josip Broz Tito's time.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how far that is the subject of this deliberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you why in just a minute. Is it true that he was thought to influence others, for example, the memorandum? It was said that he was influential in the memorandum affair of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know the kind of man that Mr. Dobrica Cosic is, that he is one of the people that advocated Serb nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All I want to ask you is this: Somebody who in 1992 and 1993, in the most difficult times for the country and accepted to be president, did that take courage?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was very sad that he was a puppet in the position he occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. What I asked you is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can comment on this, and it's purely a comment. All he can say is what the conversation was. That's his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I will get through my questions very quickly and I wouldn't have asked him about the book "Far is the Sun" or about "Deobe," "Divisions," had he not brought the subject of "Far is the Sun" up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is what you said quite literally during the examination-in-chief verbatim: Dobrica Cosic asked you to tell him about Muslim tolerance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: Does anybody know the holy scriptures better and the Koran and the history of churches, him being a writer? He's an author. Does anybody know about that better than Dobrica Cosic? And did he need to ask you to tell him about Muslim tolerance as if he didn't know about it himself?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Islamic tolerance, I'm quite sure that I was a better expert on the subject than him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, I've completed that topic. Now let's move on to the next one. You spoke about the fact that tanks crossed the Sava River bridge; right, off in some direction?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the Sava bridge and all the other bridges, are they located in the centre of Belgrade? On one embankment is the Old Belgrade and on the other side, on the other bank, is New Belgrade. So how do you know where the tanks were going?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know there was a lot of traffic and traffic jams and you could hear voices and noise all over the place, and it was quite obvious that the convoys were moving in the direction I stated. I didn't say I knew for sure. I saw what I saw on the bridges; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And another two questions: When you spoke about this professor that spoke about the genocidal Koran, could you give me the name and surname of that man? Is it possible you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the most genocidal programmes that were repeated night after night on Belgrade television. And a moment ago Mr. Milosevic asked me the Bible, Koran is always against terror, all forms of terror and violence and sexual abuse and violence against women.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come you don't remember the name and surname of the professor if you remembered all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that programme, a peace-loving neighbour of mine, a quiet man, attacked my door and said, "I had no idea the kind of bestial people live next door to me," he was so influenced by this programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now my next question: Were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that question, you know that everybody working in federal organs were always members. It was automatic. But I never dealt with communism ideology or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To the last day, that is 1990, were you a member of the League of Communists until it existed?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: Did you attend services in the mosque while you were a member of the League of Communists? You did?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just two points, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, Mr. Milosevic asked you about the composition, the changing composition of the Yugoslav army. Did you ever have a conversation with Mr. Jovanovic during which he expressed or relayed his observations about the changing composition of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember one. I knew Mr. Jovanovic. I only remember one encounter, one meeting, a chance meeting at the beginning, in fact, at the beginning of 1992. He was excited and he said that the time had come to put in the injustice done to the Serbs right and that we were entering a new era where all Serbs had their tasks to round off and create their own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic put several parts of your statement to you, and in particular he -- your assertion in your statement that you overheard Jovanovic refer to the other person on the phone as "Comrade Slobo." Did you, after coming to Holland, sit down and dictate corrections or -- that you saw in your statement? Did you attempt to correct what you perceived as mistakes in your statement?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, Your Honours, my statement is based on my recollections, and I am certain of the contents that I heard during that telephone conversation between Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Milosevic. Those -- that then was my -- was oral conveyance of orders. And then Jovanovic rang someone else up and conveyed that to them. I don't know who. But I just said what I recalled and heard in that room, sitting in a corner of it, on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking you is last week did you sit down and dictate to a member of the Office of the Prosecutor corrections to your statement, where, after reviewing your statement, you felt that some parts of the statement were incorrect? Did you do that in the last week?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As far as I recall, usually they would refer to him as "President Slobo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I'm going to ask that it be marked for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is the document that you now have before you, is that a memo containing the portions of your statement which you felt were incorrect which you corrected by dictating corrections to a member of the OTP staff?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read everything carefully, of course, and in the way Mr. Jovanovic addressed the person, as far as I can remember, he would have addressed him with "President" but also with "Comrade" too. He used the word "Drug" as well. And I'd like to say once again or, rather, in describing the room, let me say I wasn't able to take note of everything but I'm sure he was addressing Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just clarify that for us? You say now that Jovanovic used both expressions, "President" and "Comrade"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Pasic, thank you for giving your evidence. It's now concluded. You're free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That last document, Mr. Groome, you asked for it to be marked for identification. In fact, we haven't even exhibited the statement so I don't think there's much point exhibiting the corrections --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll withdraw it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- particularly in light of the last answer, which hasn't made matters much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will withdraw it and leave the oral testimony as it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, leave it as the evidence is. Thank you. Now, we're being handed some binders which we'll keep for the moment. What we'll deal with is, first of all, the application, as I understand it, that you want to make, Mr. Groome, in relation to the motions for admission of 92 bis witnesses. To explain, this concerns not those immediately upcoming witnesses, which we will come to in a moment, this concerns a motion which I think you filed on the 18th of June, and it relates to 15 witnesses who have made statements in relation to events in Bijeljina, Bratunac, and Zvornik, and I understand that you have a further application in relation to them. We will be considering that motion fairly shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that the Chamber is burdened with a great deal of work. Because of some scheduling difficulties, it appears that there may be some openings before the end of the summer break, so the Prosecution's request to the Chamber was, if it was possible, to expedite a ruling on nine of those witnesses, and if that was possible, then we could then schedule them and have them in the event that they're needed before the summer break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And can you tell us those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witnesses, Your Honour, I'm uncertain, or in exercise of caution, if possible, I would like to refer to all of them by their number so that I don't inadvertently violate any protective orders, but they are: B-1488, B-1516, B-1097, B-1010, B-1502, B-1524, B-1704, B-1460, and B-1750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you would wish, if possible, to call those, if necessary, before the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what weeks would you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's the end of the second to last week in August, and then the final week in August. There have been some problems with visas and other logistical problems with some of the witnesses. Basically to have a reserve of witnesses available so that we do not lose any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider those next. It may be we'll have an oral hearing next week on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's of assistance to the Court, the Prosecution will be conceding that cross-examination is appropriate in some of them based on the ruling -- the recent ruling we have from the Chamber. If that facilitates or expedites the Chamber's consideration of that, the Prosecution -- would you like me to deal with that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we might as well deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the following witnesses -- out of that nine, Your Honour, the Prosecution concede that there is a substantive reference to the JNA and, based upon the Chamber's ruling, cross-examination would be appropriate. And those witnesses would be 1480 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please slow down a moment, I'm going to make a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry. 1488, 1097, 1502, 1704, and 1460. The other remaining witnesses the Prosecution will be asking the Chamber to consider whether cross-examination is necessary and I can reserve my remarks to next week, if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that assistance. Five witnesses; is that right? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe I misspoke when I said six; there's five witnesses and four that we believe there's an argument to be made for cross-examination not being required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move from there to the next witnesses you propose to call. Now, these are all transcript witnesses, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are all the witnesses testifying about the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's all Foca. We've been handed a binder. No doubt it was that that Mr. Milosevic was complaining about earlier. Perhaps you would introduce it to us so we can find out what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statements and transcripts of most of these witnesses were disclosed over a year ago, on the 1st of June, 2002. The entire package that we will now be seeking to introduce was submitted on the first -- on the 10th of January of this year in the form of three binders of exhibits plus the transcripts. To assist the Chamber, and particularly to assist the accused, we are redisclosing the package as it pertains to each witness just before the witness in the event that it is of assistance to the accused, which I believe, during the Kosovo portion of the case, it was indicated to the Prosecution that that was of assistance. So it is not a matter of newly delivered material that the accused has not had an opportunity to review but simply of us attempting to facilitate his handling of a large amount of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what I seem to have here is, looking at the binder, it's the transcript of D-1536, who is in fact -- is that right? He's in fact unprotected; am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Avdic. So he's the next witness. So we find his transcript at tab 1. Are there then the various exhibits which he produced; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Following tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the following tabs are the exhibits which we would seek to introduce. If I could also just note, many of these witnesses were subject to some various forms of protection in closed session so we've put a surrogate sheet to indicate that a redacted copy of this testimony is available from the ICTY website rather than burden the Court again with a separate redacted copy of the transcript. So that's been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So we've got -- but so that I can make sure that we've got -- so these aren't necessarily exhibits produced by this particular witness but by the generality of Foca witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The package that you have before you are the exhibits produced by this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the exception we are not seeking to reintroduce videos that were introduced in the original trial. We do not feel it's necessary. But they are indicated at tabs 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, with respect to this bundle of exhibits, there were statements of this witness introduced on -- during cross-examination. The Prosecution takes no strong position on whether they should be put before this Chamber. We thought, in fairness, that we would include them. I do note that Mr. Kay did raise objection to them and we'll simply be guided by the Chamber's wish in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are prior statements of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Prior statements were introduced during the cross-examination to impeach, I imagine, the credibility of the witness. Mr. Kay was objecting to the introduction of that prior statement in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would have thought the whole passage should go in, including those statements if they were used to impeach the witness. That would seem to be right. But the point going back to what Mr. Milosevic was complaining of earlier, the point is that these are merely the documents which have been disclosed earlier, indeed, when we considered the application. They had been disclosed. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. These --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But merely rearranged in a more convenient form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: These were disclosed over six months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And disclosed over a year ago in a different format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this witness, you're proposing to call him, summarise the transcript, is that right, and then leave him for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, next to me is Ms. Melissa Pack who is the person -- the lawyer, who has assembled all the Foca witnesses. With the Court's permission, I'd ask that she be allowed to assist us and take this witness and some of the other Foca witnesses that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wouldn't like to repeat anything that Mr. Kay has conveyed. They are our common commission -- positions regarding 92 bis witnesses and everything else, but a technical problem has arisen. A few days ago unfortunately, an associate from the OTP, Ms. Stefanie, took all the statements from the Foca witnesses because they were incomplete, and as an amicus, I did not have in my possession the statement of the witness that we are going to hear now. That will not be an obstacle; I read it earlier on. But this does cause difficulties, because I couldn't devote my attention to the statements of these witnesses in the coming period over the past two days because I didn't have the documents with me, and this is a cause of difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there are any matters on which you need to cross-examine, I'm sure that they can emerge during the cross-examination by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I sit down if I can make one more comment about this group of witnesses. The Prosecution is proposing that after the witnesses who for cross-examination is required, after they complete their testimony that we then tender the transcripts of those witnesses for which cross-examination was not required. In that way, the Chamber would have in consecutive exhibit numbers, all of the evidence related to Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very we will. We need an exhibit number for this particular binder. Yes. The next Prosecution Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, would you give the Court, please, your name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Safet Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Avdic, have you testified on two previous occasions in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And did you testify on the first occasion in the case of Kunarac on the 22nd and 23rd of March of 2000?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the second occasion in the case of Krnojelac on the 1st and 2nd of November, 2000?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, of the transcripts and exhibits in those proceedings can be admitted as the -- admitted in evidence save for the tabs that have been identified by Mr. Groome as 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. They are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose to read out a summary of the evidence in those two proceedings. In Prosecutor and Kunarac, the witness testified about the SDA and SDS founding rallies in Foca and the ethnic composition of different neighbourhoods in Foca. He said that when the war began, looking from his apartment he could see military activity on the hill Dub and men wearing former Yugoslav army-type closing. He saw a machine-gun pointed towards Foca. Shortly before the war, the witness saw people walking around Foca with weapons. He heard that Serbs were organising militarily. He did not hear the same of Muslims. Serb women and children were leaving Foca on buses before the attack. On the 8th of April, the shooting started. Later on, the witness saw soldiers on the street in front of his house wearing uniforms of the old Yugoslav army, all carrying weapons. Some of the soldiers were locals from Foca. Some came from elsewhere. He learned later these were paramilitary units from Serbia, the White Eagles, and Arkan's people. Some also came from Montenegro. Local soldiers were exclusively Serb. Foca was taken by the Serbs around mid-April. From his apartment, the witness says he saw shelling and troop movement in vehicles in the direction of the Gorazde. The Serb army was using these vehicles. He saw aeroplanes moving in the direction of Gorazde. He saw parts of Foca burning. All of the houses that he saw burning were owned by Muslims. In May one or two houses would be burning per day. He visited Donje Polje, a Muslim neighbourhood and saw the mosque there burning. He says all the mosques in Foca were destroyed during the war. On the 19th of May, the witness was addressed. He was taken to KP Dom. He would stay there for almost 900 days. The men who were confined with him were all Muslims. He describes the living conditions at KP Dom. He says that some of the prisoners were taken out for forced labour. He describes groups of men being taken out to the office in the administrative building. He says cries and blows could be heard and sometimes shots. Between June and July, five or six groups were taken out. All the men are still missing. The witness gave evidence that his group of about 15 people were always concealed from the International Red Cross. It was only towards the end of December 1993 that the Red Cross were allowed to visit them. The first time the Red Cross visited was in June or July 1992, and they returned on several occasions before the witness and his group were registered. The witness was finally released from KP Dom on the 5th of October, 1994, and exchanged on the 6th of October, 1994. He did not have contact with his family from 1992 until the beginning of January 1995. And then to summarise in the Krnojelac proceedings, the witness described again the living conditions in KP Dom. He describes the overcrowded bedrooms with mattresses only, solitary confinement cells without heating, that visitors were not allowed. He describes the treatment of Serb regular prisoners in contrast to the Muslim detainees. He testifies that some detainees were forced to work even if sick. The witness saw detainees being taken away on several occasions according to lists drawn up in advance. He heard cries and shots. On one occasion he saw the lights of a vehicle moving over the Drina and later the sound of something like sandbags hitting the water. Some detainees who worked in the auto repair shop told the witness they saw traces of blood inside this vehicle after the events described. The witness never saw the detainees who were taken out in this way again. Detainees were taken out and told they would be exchanged but were never seen again. Other detainees were taken out and told they were to pick plums but were never seen again. The witness had only limited access to medical treatment. While in KP Dom he suffered from heart problems due to lack of medication and other physical conditions associated with the cold and lack of hygiene. In the two or three months at the very beginning, he lost 40 kilos. He describes being scared to death in KP Dom. He is still suffering severely from the psychological effects of his detention. And that is a summary of the evidence in the earlier proceedings. I don't propose to ask the witness any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters did not hear the beginning. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you start again. The interpreters did not hear the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Avdic, on page 2, paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that the Serbian Democratic Party, in the summer of 1990, held a public rally at the stadium in Foca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it, however, true that the first public political rally held in Foca was the one held by the SDA, organised by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was quite some time before this rally of the Serbian Democratic Party, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Two months before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So first there was the SDA rally. Is it true that the Foca municipality is the largest municipality in terms of territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that in the territory of Foca municipality there were less than 50.000 inhabitants living there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the ethnic composition was such that there were 53 per cent Muslims and 47 per cent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Fifty-two per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, 52 per cent Muslims and 48 per cent Serbs. And tell me, please, is it true that at the rally of the Serbian Democratic Party that you referred to, there were about 10.000 people, mostly local Serbs? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that at the rally of the Party of Democratic Action, which was held before that on the Drina riverbank, there were about 100.000 men present?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many people were present?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Maybe some 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, 20.000. And there was a total of 20.000 Muslims living in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: 52 per cent, which makes it 25.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Very well. But is it also correct that at the SDA rally in Foca - this is according to information that I have, - there were 100.000 people present, but is it true there were tens of thousands of Muslims from Serbia, from Sandzak led by Sulejman Ugljanin?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I number is certainly not that high. Now, whether there were people from Serbia, from Sandzak, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the rally was addressed by Alija Izetbegovic, among others?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were present at that rally?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: For a brief period at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it lasted quite -- for some time. How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: For some 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the speech of Alija Izetbegovic here. I will have it in due course. But since attention has been drawn to tab 15, we have established, therefore, that according to my information, there were ten times more Muslims attending the SDA rally than the Serbs attending the other rally. You say there were twice as many, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going it over again. It's disputed. We've got his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do have his evidence. He says 20 or so thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this tab 15, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Semso Tankosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make sure the witness has it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, there isn't a transcript of it in B/C/S. I think it was a video that was admitted by the Defence in that case and obviously in B/C/S and a transcript was only provided in English. So I don't think much purpose will be served by showing it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's get it interpreted. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the witness will hear it. It's very brief, because this is an abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Semso Tankosic," in brackets, it says, "President of the Executive Board of the SDA for Zagreb." He's a Muslim, isn't he, and President of the Executive Board for the SDA in Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But listen to his speech. He says: [In English] "Are we Serbs? (Crowd: No.) Are we maybe Croats? (Crowd: No.) Are we Muslims? (Crowd: Yes.)" [Interpretation] Then he says: "Dear gentlemen, honoured reporters. Dear friends..." [In English] "Serbs and Croats. Here you had the opportunity to hear how on behalf of 3 million Muslims the people gathered here answered who we are and what we are. We are Muslims and don't you ever forget it. (Cheering crowd) This is also an answer to all those that, for whichever petty political reasons they might have, declare themselves Serbs or Croats though they belong to the Islamic religion, and that say that SDA doesn't suit them because it is an excessively green party. I tell them from this spot: 'It should be green. It's ours.'" [Interpretation] That is what we find in this tab that was provided to me. As for Izetbegovic's speech, I assume you heard it.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: A part of it. Not all of it. I said that I was there for some 20 minutes. While the rally was opened, then maybe up to ten minutes I listened to Izetbegovic, and then I left. I was quite to the side, close to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this, in your opinion, a nationalist rally?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No, because there were Serbs present at that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. But you heard the speech. Isn't this a nationalist speech?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Avdic. Since you say there were Serbs at the rally, is it true that there wasn't a single Serb flag but only Muslim flags and one or two Croat?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I didn't pay any attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, if we have established when your rally was held and that after that was a rally of the Serbian Democratic Party was held in Foca at which, in your assessment too, there were far fewer people, do you consider this to mark the beginning of hostilities in the territory of Foca?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: First of all, that -- first of all, that was not my rally. I am not a member of the SDA. I respected all faiths and all ethnicities, and I socialised with everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Avdic. This is certainly praiseworthy, but that is not my question. Why do you consider the rally of the Serbian Democratic Party in Foca, which took place later and was much smaller in size, to mark the beginning of hostilities in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: That is not stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was not the beginning of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: That is not stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says that he didn't say it, so you can't attribute it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'm moving on. I'm not arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on then, Mr. Avdic, to the next point. On page 2, paragraph 5, you say that you personally did not see but you heard that local Serbs, several months prior to the beginning of the war, had started to organise military units and that they had started military training at Vucevo near Tjentiste; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it, however, true that the first organised arming of ethnic groups in the territory of Foca first took place among Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No. On the basis of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before I quote from your statement, let me read to you from tab 16. I think it's from tab 16. This is a newspaper article. Cengic is making a statement for the newspaper Ljiljan. You've heard of that. 18th to the 25th of May, 1998 is that issue of the Liljan or The Lily. So I'll read to you only one paragraph on page 3 of this very lengthy interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can have this document. We've probably got the original. Yes. Which page, page 3?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no pagination, but it's the third piece of paper in this tab. There's a photograph first, then interview of the week, and the third page with the photograph again but of a smaller size of the person interviewed. The far right column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is linked to what I was saying, that they started arming first. Here is what Cengic says: "Foca was the centre for arming. From there, several thousand barrels were distributed across Bosnia and Herzegovina from Ljubinje to Srebrenica. Even Naser Oric would come for the weapons." Cengic says: "I don't know whether it was the centre, but we did assist various municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina as far as we could. And when those weapons reached Foca, no one could know about it and still less receive it in his home. Sajo --" and his name is Senad Sahinpasic, Sajo. You probably know that man, don't you? You've heard of Senad Sahinpasic, Sajo?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Sajo complained to me and I said to him, Drive it to my home, and that is what we did. So the problem was not in the weapons but in the consciousness of people and in the organisation." End of quote. So that a large part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was supplied with weapons from there means that not only were the people of Foca being armed but they supplied other municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina with weapons. And then he goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait. Wait. The witness must have the chance to deal with this. You're putting it to him. Now, Mr. Avdic -- wait --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not claiming, I'm just reading. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It's what's in the interview, but he should have a chance of dealing with it. Can you assist us with what's in the interview and what the accused has read out, Mr. Avdic, whether as far as you know that was the case, there was arming from Foca? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about it, nor do I believe it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on at the bottom of the paragraph it says: "There was criticism at your expense and Saja's that you gained wealth, but I won't dwell on that. I don't want to waste time on that." And then in the last line on that page it says: "It should be known that in those times, it was risky, to drive weapons, to stockpile it, to distribute it and the like. One could be arrested any time. Saja with the assistance of some men from Focatrans," which is a company, isn't it, a transport company there in Foca, isn't it, Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Focatrans, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "He would take people, procure weapons, drive them in encountering thousands of problems," et cetera, et cetera. Therefore, isn't it beyond doubt that there was a large concentration of weapons among the Muslims in Foca in a period that preceded the conflicts that you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: That's not true. As far as I know, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, Mr. May, that famous sentence, "There are many things in this world that your mind does not even dream of, Horatio." You know that because it's Shakespeare, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're certainly not going into Shakespeare. You're cross-examining this witness, rather than addressing a literary class. Just examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he didn't know about it. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But on page 2, paragraph 5, you say that you saw with the Muslims some kinds of rifles. "I saw some rifles with the Muslims, and some Muslims who had money bought weapons." Is that what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes, hunting rifles, hunting knives. And later on, some people did purchase something. But exclusively hunting rifles, hunting knives and hunting equipment, which later on in the houses in which I lived in the centre and where I lived, the militia, the military police would come in to search the flats and confiscate the weapons without issuing any receipts testifying to the confiscation of these weapons and their ultimate return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Avdic, not to waste time. Do you only claim you saw hunting rifles, nothing else, no other rifles, just hunting rifles? Is that you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: That the Muslims had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, as you said -- you went on to say they purchased rifles. Who did they purchase rifles from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know if the Muslims had in their possession some other kinds of weapons other than the rifles you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I heard about that. I heard that they had something like mortars for the expulsion of shells, small shells. And in my previous statement, I said that that was in the area of Sukovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Sukovac is a hill near Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: An elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: On the left bank of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Now, on page 2, paragraph 6 of your own statement, you say that the Muslims had several cannons; is that right, guns?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: That's what I said but I didn't see what these weapons were, but from what a Serb was saying, a Serb from Foca, that the shells that were shelling the area from those -- that weaponry did not explode. And on the basis of the tale told by him, I used the word cannon or gun, but I didn't actually see those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the shells that were expulsed from those weapons, they didn't know how to remove the protective shell, to ignite the shell and that's why they didn't explode. They weren't handled properly. I assume you know that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, now you see how well they were trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me how many cannons you referred to. You say several guns or cannons?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was one or two. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say one or two.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I didn't actually see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they got those cannons from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Avdic. Now, does it emerge from all this, from the quotation by Cengic and from what you're saying about the cannons, I assume cannons are not hunting cannons. If you say rifles are hunting rifles, I don't assume that cannons can be hunting cannons. Is it therefore clear that the Muslims of the Foca municipality, far before the Serbs, began to organise themselves militarily?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's not right either? All right.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: As far as I know. To the best of my knowledge, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right i. I'm sure you knew that the Muharem Cengic said in the newspaper called Liljan said that the Muslims of the Foca region, even before the conflict broke out, had organised themselves into armed military formations -- into combat military formations.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't re -- read about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you at least know this: That far before the conflict broke out the SDA party, the SDA party organised armed night patrols which monitored the movements of the local Serbs? You must have noticed that as an inhabitant of Foca yourself.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: From Cajnici, the arrival of individual Serbs, leaders, this was attended. They were armed with short machine-guns, those short machine-guns and they would come in and pass by through the town along with some of the local Foca Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Did you yourself see armed patrols of the SDA party, the Muslim party? That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see them. I mentioned to you a moment ago the man that was nicknamed Saja and his name was actually Senad Sahinpasic. You know him, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that this man before the war sold and resold various goods and later on he was commander of the local Muslim units, wasn't he? That's right, isn't it? Was he later on the commander of local Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But if I may just add something to the previous question, the sale of goods. He had a registered company for the trading with fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you claim that he wasn't commander of the Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that either?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. And let me state again I was not a member of the SDA party or any kind of activist in the SDA or of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you weren't an activist in the SDS either. And you're testifying against the Serbs. And you know nothing about the SDA. Is that right, Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the structure of the leadership cadres, armaments and things like that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Avdic, that the first barricade with armed personnel in Foca was organised precisely on the Muslim side and that by this man Saja, nicknamed Saja, you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember what happened in the central part of Foca, in the centre of town called Donje Polje in the direction of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was there a barricade erected there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't move around town at that time. I lived in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's in the centre of town. Donje Polje, isn't that the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No. The centre is the hotel and the region around Drina and Ceotina where the Maglic enterprise is located, that's the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is Donje Polje from that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Maybe 200 metres, 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 200 to 300 metres from where you were and you don't know there was a barricade there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't move in that radius of 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Not at the time you're asking me about, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, you say on page 2, paragraph 6, that the Serbs started the attack on Foca on the 7th of April, 1992; isn't that right, Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you yourself lived in Foca at the time and you're testifying about that, and not for the first time, if I understand it correctly, Mr. Avdic; is that right? You're a frequent witness for the opposing side over there.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I have already state that had to the Tribunal, to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm sure you know why the attack on Foca took place at all and the conflict in Foca took place at all, how it came about. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why the attack was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true and correct, I assume that was common knowledge at the time and I assume you knew about it too, that the Serbs broke into a coded Muslim message that had been sent which this man Senad Sahinpasic, "Saja," sent to the Muslim forces under arms. And that message was that the Muslims should start the attack and that message was intercepted. You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 6, you also say that the attacks were launched by Serb soldiers from Pljevlje and Niksic together with the local Serbs, members of the White Eagles and the Serb guards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this, please: In those conflicts and clashes in Foca, did a single member of the JNA take part, a single unit of the JNA? Did it take part?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: The army uniforms were those of the Yugoslav army. It was army uniforms of the Yugoslav army and camouflage military uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avdic, I'm not asking you the kinds of uniforms. I'm asking you whether it is true that there were paramilitary units who on the basis of self-organisation were included in the struggles around Foca, and I'm asking you quite precisely: Is it true that there was not a single JNA soldier who was in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I saw people wearing military uniforms of the JNA. That's what I saw. And I also saw people wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, these White Eagles and the Serb guards, the Serb guard, the SPO, the ones you mention, are they also paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: From what people tell me. But there was a great deal of coordination between those units and the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Did you bear in mind at all the fact that these units also wore uniforms that were the same as military uniforms? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not quite sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serb guard, the SPO and the White Eagles, do they belong to the JNA? Let me put it that way. Are they JNA units?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can only deal with what he saw himself. Did you see any -- you may be able to answer this, but did you see any coordination, that's what is put, between any VJ or JNA units and the paramilitaries? It may be, as I say, you can't answer that, but if you did see, perhaps you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to say this. That coordination, I linked it up -- that was the conclusion I drew as to coordination. The attack on Jelec was first done by planes. Jelec was bombed from the air. After that it was heavy artillery that went in to shell it from the Karlovac axis, direction, and after all that there was an infantry attack on Jelec. And from that, I deduced, I draw the conclusion that there was coordination of this entire operation between the JNA and the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in Foca, you actually only saw paramilitary units. Isn't that right, Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: And people wearing the uniform of the Yugoslav Army with weapons, rifles, and machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The people that you denote as paramilitary units, did they also wear the clothing, the uniforms of that Yugoslav People's Army, as you refer to it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I said camouflage uniforms. I saw people wearing clothing of the Yugoslav People's Army and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the non-camouflage ones, those were the ones used by the Territorial Defence. Isn't that right, Mr. Avdic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the general olive-green uniforms, that was the standard type of uniform that the Territorial Defence had, and each of the Territorial Defence people had a uniform like that at home.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: That equipment had been withdrawn a year previously from the warehouses and depots of the TO, and it had been -- it was taken off in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go into that question here and now with you. I don't think you'll be able to give us much assistance in that respect. Let me just ask you this: Is it true that for a full 20 or more years from Foca the JNA garrison was moved out, there was no garrison left in Foca, and that the nearest JNA unit was at a distance of 12 kilometres from Foca, in a village called Filipovici? Isn't that right? As a man from Foca yourself, you must know that.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know when it was dislodged, but was disbanded from there and there is the village of Filipovici, and it was engaged militarily. Now, what the organisation of the units was there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the nearest one was 12 kilometres away in the village of Filipovici. And is it true that this was a unit which was exclusively there because there was just a fuel depot there and the quartermaster supplies and no weapons at all?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they had down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that there were only 12 soldiers that manned the area and kept guard over this fuel depot and the quartermaster equipment, such as blankets, rucksacks, and the rest of it, just 12 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at the head of the facility, that is to say the sole military facility 12 kilometres away from Foca and Filipovici, was a Muslim who was a major by rank and his name was Muharem Kurtovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either? Well, do you know, for example, that these local forces in Foca, the paramilitaries too, and even these 12 soldiers, members of the JNA that provided security for the depot as well as Major Kurtovic, that they were disarmed and transported the next day with only their sidearms to Montenegro and sent off to Montenegro the very next day. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Major Kurtovic himself, during these conflicts, offered shelter within that JNA depot to numerous men, women, and children who took refuge from the attack, took shelter there?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but I can't say for sure; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have any knowledge about the fact that any of these JNA soldiers took part in the battle for Foca at all? Was a single bullet shot?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know of a single soldier that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that the fighting went on for eight days, up until the 16th of April, 1992? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear on what you mean, Your Honours. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you told us when the conflict began; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you mean in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Foca. And the fighting went on for eight days, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how long the fighting went on for. I didn't say eight days myself, but about eight or ten days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I wanted to hear from you. Whether it was eight or ten days, it doesn't matter, it's not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be a convenient moment. I see it's 12.15. Mr. Avdic, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you remember, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence during the adjournment, and that does include the members of the Prosecution. Could you be back in 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recollect that Muslim forces, during these conflicts, held positions in a part of town or the hill known as Sukovac?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything at all about the scope of those forces holding that hill?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that the position -- there were positions also within the KP Dom, that is Muslim positions? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any positions. The KP Dom held prisoners from the period of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not asking you about that. It is -- there is no doubt that people were serving their prison sentences in the KP Dom. I'm asking you whether there were Muslim positions, which means armed units, Muslim units within the compound of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what kind of weapon was used at Sukovac to open fire on Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I can only make assumptions. Shells fell on the upper part of Cohodar Mahala, and I was told this by a Serb because we visited each other after Foca fell, and he told me the Serbs were all laughing because not a single one of those shells went off. And that is what I know and what is for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But do you know that those were howitzers that they had on that hill of Sukovac, that the Muslim forces had howitzers?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said a moment ago that I didn't know which weapons they had. I only know that he told me that there were shells. Now, what weapons were used to fire them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, do you know anything at all as to where those forces got those weapons from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET AVDIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
